name: Zinc-based deodorant (Zinc ricinoleate)

card.summary: Castor-oil zinc salt in deodorants that claims to adsorb odor; mechanism unclear, no trials.
card.note: Safety data not found in reviewed sources.

quick.overview:
Zinc ricinoleate is an ingredient in many deodorants, where it is described as adsorbing odor rather than masking it.

Its mechanism is described as unclear, and no clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: Said to bind odor molecules; a 2000 simulation study examined the adsorption.
quick.risks: Safety information was not found in the reviewed sources.

lead: Zinc ricinoleate is the zinc salt of ricinoleic acid, the main fatty acid in castor oil. It is used in many deodorants as an odor adsorber: it is said to bind smelly molecules rather than mask them or stop sweating. People choose zinc-based deodorants as a way to smell clean without aluminium antiperspirants, since body odor strongly affects how a person is perceived up close. [1][2]

Deodorants in general work by covering odor or limiting the bacteria that produce it, while antiperspirants reduce sweat, usually with aluminium salts. [3] A 1983 comparison study of underarm deodorants reported that zinc ricinoleate, as an odor absorber, reduced the perceived malodor for up to 24 hours in trained-assessor testing. [4]

Wikipedia states that the mechanism of its odor adsorption is unclear and cites a 2000 computer simulation study of it. [1] Allergic contact dermatitis has been reported in case reports, including to zinc ricinoleate in a deodorant marketed as natural. [5][6]

chain: Deodorant with zinc ricinoleate is applied to the underarm
Odor molecules are adsorbed while sweat is left alone
angle.text: Zinc ricinoleate deodorants are used to reduce body odor as part of a grooming routine. Users who prefer to keep sweating but control smell look to this ingredient as an alternative to aluminium antiperspirants.

infobox: Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel assessed zinc salts as safe when formulated to be non-irritating [7]

paras: Zinc ricinoleate is found in many deodorants as an adsorber of odor. [1] Deodorants generally work by masking odor or limiting the bacteria that break down sweat; antiperspirants go further by reducing sweating, typically through aluminium salts that plug sweat ducts. Early commercial deodorants used zinc oxide among other ingredients. [3]

A dermatology review of antiperspirant and deodorant ingredients lists zinc ricinoleate among substances meant to bind offending smells, alongside perfumes, antibacterials such as triclosan, and pH-influencing agents. [2] Zinc ricinoleate has also been tested as an odor-control additive in ostomy pouches, where a 2024 study found products containing it, with and without orange terpenes, were assessed for odor intensity and pleasantness; the version with orange terpenes scored far lower in malodor. [8]

In the 1983 International Journal of Cosmetic Science study, double-blind crossover trials with trained assessors found that ethanol reduced underarm odor for up to 24 hours, that adding antimicrobials increased the effect, and that zinc ricinoleate reduced the perception of existing malodor for up to 24 hours. [4]

The Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety reviewed 27 zinc salts used in cosmetics and concluded they are safe in present practices of use and concentration when formulated to be non-irritating. [7] A 2007 safety assessment covered ricinoleic acid and its salts, including zinc ricinoleate, as skin-conditioning agents and surfactants in cosmetics. [9]
Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to zinc ricinoleate in deodorants, in 2001 and again in 2024 in a product marketed as natural. [5][6]

A 1983 double-blind, trained-assessor study of underarm deodorants included zinc ricinoleate as an odor absorber and reported reduced perceived malodor for up to 24 hours. [4] No modern randomized trial of zinc-ricinoleate deodorants against other products was found.

timeline.event: Study of underarm deodorants reports zinc ricinoleate reducing perceived malodor. [4]
Contact dermatitis case report links zinc ricinoleate in a deodorant to allergy. [6]
Expert panel completes safety assessment of zinc salts in cosmetics; further allergy case report published. [5][7]
